prompt: How did chemists at the Dow Chemical Company prepare phenol on an industrial scale from chlorobenzene?

choices.text: By treating chlorobenzene with dilute aqueous NaOH at 340 °C under 170 atm pressure
By treating chlorobenzene with aqueous NaOH at room temperature
choices.why: Without electron-withdrawing groups, chlorobenzene doesn't react with nucleophiles under ordinary conditions. High temperature and pressure are needed.

choices.text: By nitrating chlorobenzene and then reducing the nitro group
choices.why: Nitration and reduction would give an amine, not phenol. The Dow process forces chlorobenzene to react with NaOH.

choices.text: By direct hydroxylation of benzene with O2 and an enzyme cofactor
choices.why: Direct hydroxylation is difficult and rarely done in the laboratory. The Dow process starts from chlorobenzene and NaOH.

explanation: Halobenzenes without electron-withdrawing substituents don't react with nucleophiles under most conditions, but at high temperature and pressure even chlorobenzene can be forced to react. In 1928, Dow chemists found that phenol could be made by treating chlorobenzene with dilute aqueous NaOH at 340 °C under 170 atm pressure.

prompt: In the Dow process, chlorobenzene is converted to phenol with dilute aqueous NaOH at 340 °C. Under what pressure, in atm?
explanation: The Dow Chemical Company's 1928 process treats chlorobenzene with dilute aqueous NaOH at 340 °C under 170 atm pressure. Such harsh conditions are needed because chlorobenzene has no electron-withdrawing groups to activate it.

prompt: What product forms when bromobenzene is treated with potassium amide (KNH2) in liquid NH3?

choices.text: Aniline
Benzene
choices.why: The bromine is replaced by an amino group, not by hydrogen.

choices.text: Phenol
choices.why: Phenol forms when the nucleophile is hydroxide or water. With KNH2 in NH3, the product is aniline.

choices.text: p-Bromoaniline
choices.why: The bromine is lost; the amino group ends up in its place or on the neighboring carbon, giving aniline.

explanation: Strong bases other than NaOH cause a similar substitution: treatment of bromobenzene with potassium amide (KNH2) in liquid NH3 gives aniline. The reaction goes through a benzyne intermediate.

prompt: When bromobenzene labeled with ^14C at carbon 1 reacts with KNH2 in NH3, where does the label end up in the aniline product?

choices.text: Equally at carbon 1 and carbon 2
Only at carbon 1, the carbon that bears the amino group
choices.why: The label is split equally between carbon 1 and carbon 2, which shows the amino group can add to either end of a symmetrical intermediate.

choices.text: Only at carbon 2, next to the amino group
choices.why: Half of the product has the label at carbon 1 and half at carbon 2.

choices.text: Spread equally over all six ring carbons
choices.why: Only carbon 1 and carbon 2 carry the label, because only those two carbons become equivalent in the intermediate.

explanation: The substitution product has equal amounts of the label at carbon 1 and carbon 2. That implies a symmetrical reaction intermediate in which carbon 1 and carbon 2 are equivalent: benzyne. NH2− (or NH3) can add to either end of its triple bond.

prompt: Bromobenzene labeled with ^14C at carbon 1 is treated with KNH2 in liquid NH3. What percentage of the aniline formed has the amino group on the labeled carbon?
explanation: The label ends up in equal amounts at carbon 1 (the carbon bearing –NH2) and carbon 2. So 50% of the aniline has the amino group on the labeled carbon, and 50% has it on the carbon next to the label.

prompt: When bromobenzene is treated with KNH2 in the presence of a conjugated diene such as furan, a Diels–Alder reaction occurs. What does this show?

choices.text: The symmetrical intermediate is benzyne, formed by elimination of HBr from bromobenzene
The intermediate is a Meisenheimer complex, formed by addition of NH2−
choices.why: A Meisenheimer complex isn't a dienophile. Trapping by a diene shows the intermediate has a triple bond: benzyne.

choices.text: The intermediate is an aryl cation, formed by loss of Br−
choices.why: Aryl cations are too unstable to form. The Diels–Alder trap shows a benzyne made by elimination of HBr.

choices.text: Furan acts as the nucleophile that replaces bromine
choices.why: Furan reacts as the diene in a Diels–Alder cycloaddition with benzyne, not as a nucleophile.

explanation: Trapping experiments give further evidence. With a conjugated diene such as furan present, a Diels–Alder reaction occurs, implying that the symmetrical intermediate is a benzyne formed by elimination of HBr. Benzyne is too reactive to isolate; with water it adds to give phenol, and with a diene it undergoes Diels–Alder cycloaddition.

prompt: What is the hybridization of the two carbons of the benzyne triple bond?

choices.text: sp2
sp, like the carbons of a typical alkyne
choices.why: A typical alkyne uses sp carbons, but benzyne's carbons stay sp2 hybridized within the ring.

choices.text: sp3
choices.why: sp3 carbons can't form π bonds. The benzyne carbons are sp2.

choices.text: One sp and one sp2
choices.why: Both carbons of the benzyne triple bond are sp2 hybridized.

explanation: Benzyne's electronic structure is that of a highly distorted alkyne. Although a typical alkyne triple bond uses sp-hybridized carbons, the benzyne triple bond uses sp2-hybridized carbons (Figure 16.7.1).

prompt: How do the two π bonds of the benzyne “triple bond” differ from those of a typical alkyne?

choices.text: One π bond is formed by p–p overlap, and the other by weak sp2–sp2 overlap in the plane of the ring
Both are formed by p–p overlap and are mutually perpendicular, as in any alkyne
choices.why: That describes a typical alkyne. In benzyne, the second π bond comes from overlap of two sp2 orbitals.

choices.text: Both are formed by sp2–sp2 overlap above and below the ring
choices.why: One π bond is the ordinary p–p overlap of the aromatic ring; only the other uses sp2 orbitals, in the plane of the ring.

choices.text: One is formed by sp–sp overlap and is unusually strong
choices.why: The extra bond comes from sp2–sp2 overlap and is very weak.

explanation: A typical alkyne triple bond has two mutually perpendicular π bonds formed by p–p overlap. The benzyne triple bond has one π bond formed by p–p overlap and one formed by sp2–sp2 overlap. The latter π bond lies in the plane of the ring and is very weak.

prompt: Treatment of m-bromotoluene with NaOH at high temperature gives a mixture of products. How many different products form?
explanation: Exercise 16.7.1: m-bromotoluene can form two different benzyne intermediates, because HBr can be eliminated using the hydrogen on either side of the bromine. Addition to these two benzynes gives three products, the methyl group being ortho, meta, or para to the new OH group.

prompt: Treatment of p-bromotoluene with NaOH at 300 °C gives two products, but m-bromotoluene gives three. Why?

choices.text: Only one benzyne can form from p-bromotoluene, but two different benzynes can form from m-bromotoluene
p-Bromotoluene reacts by nucleophilic addition through a Meisenheimer complex, and m-bromotoluene through benzyne
choices.why: Neither ring has an electron-withdrawing group to stabilize a Meisenheimer complex; both react through benzyne intermediates.

choices.text: The methyl group directs the nucleophile meta in p-bromotoluene but ortho and para in m-bromotoluene
choices.why: Directing effects for electrophiles aren't the explanation. The count depends on how many benzynes can form.

choices.text: m-Bromotoluene also loses its methyl group, giving phenol as a third product
choices.why: The methyl group stays on the ring. The extra product comes from a second benzyne intermediate.

explanation: Exercise 16.7.1: in p-bromotoluene the two hydrogens next to the bromine are equivalent, so only one benzyne forms, and OH− adds to either end of it to give two products. In m-bromotoluene the two hydrogens next to the bromine differ, so two different benzynes form, giving three products in all.
